newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks to mark restructuring in 1996 reports.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks to mark restructuring in 1996 reports.

text.p: Switzerland's three global banks should reveal the progress of expensive restructuring efforts launched last year when they report on 1996 results starting on Friday, analysts say.
Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) will open the annual reporting season this week followed by Credit Suisse Group on March 5 and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) on March 12.

Analysts said few surprises were likely because all three banks gave detailed forecasts late last year of extraordinary losses for major restructuring plans, including big write-offs for domestic loans gone bad due to a stagnant economy.

"All three big banks have more or less announced what we should expect for the full year (1996)....There won't be many surprises or deviations from what they have said," said Claudia von Tuerk at Geneva-based Pictet & Cie.

John Leonard at Salomon Brothers in London said attention now was tuned to progress and prospects for 1997. "I think we'll be looking more to the commentary on how 1997 has started (and) any trends," he told Reuters.
Both Leonard and von Tuerk said an important detail in the 1996 numbers would be how much costs rose due to high salaries and bonuses in the competitive field of investment banking.

"Expense trends have been an issue at all the investment banks, but most notably with CS Group last year. The overall trend of expense growth was certainly one of the suprises in the first half figures (for 1996)," Leonard said.

At issue for this year is when the banks, which have been struggling to boost profitability to keep up with U.S., British and continental European competitors, will start seeing these improvements from their multi-billion Swiss franc restructuring efforts.

Credit Suisse and SBC last year started reorganising their global businesses in core areas and changed the way they set provisions for risky loans, including setting aside big one-time reserves to clean bad old loans from their books.

Credit Suisse said it expected to take an extraordinary charge of 3.9 billion francs ($2.6 billion) for a 1996 loss of 2.1 billion, while SBC wrote off 3.3 billion francs for an estimated extraordinary loss of 1.9 billion.
UBS, while not revamping its provisioning methods, took a three billion franc charge to cover credit risk and domestic restructuring, resulting in a 1996 loss of about 500 million francs.

"They have all said what they will do by restructuring," said Susanne Borer at Bank Vontobel in Zurich. "Now we want to see how they are doing it, how far they have come with cutting jobs and what is the remaining timeframe."

Analysts also said they wanted to know if the domestic credit risk situation had worsened or might be improving. A weaker Swiss franc and limited growth in Europe may give the export-dependent Swiss economy a boost in 1997 after six years of stagnation.
Six analysts polled at Swiss and London banks forecast on average that UBS would report a loss per bearer share of 18.5 Swiss francs for 1996 and earnings of 96.5 francs in 1997.
The corresponding numbers for Credit Suisse were minus 11.2 in 1996 and plus 12.05 in 1997. SBC was seen reporting a loss per share of 25.2 francs for last year and earnings of 22.6 francs for 1997.
